list.listitem: The diagnosis of anal fistula depends primarily on the history and physical examination (including examination under anesthesia if needed). Additional tests are only required for suspected complex fistulae and can include fistulography, MRI, endoanal ultrasound, and/or CT. C
Examination under anesthesia combined with endoanal ultrasound or MRI are currently recommended in patient's with Crohn's disease. C
Treatment can include management of symptoms with watchful waiting in asymptomatic fistula C or surgical interventions based on the location and associated symptoms. B
Pharmacologic therapy (antibiotics with or without immunomodulators) with or without surgery is moderately effective in patients with Crohn's disease and complex or recurrent fistulae. B
Prognosis for resolution with maintenance of function is good for simple fistulae but poor in patients with complex or recurrent fistulae. B

background.definition: Anorectal fistula is a tract lined with epithelium or granulation tissue from an opening inside the anal canal to an opening in the skin. Categorization depends on its location: intersphincteric, low transsphincteric (internal opening at or below the dentate line), high transsphincteric (internal opening above the dentate line), suprasphincteric, or extrasphincteric (Parks classification). Fistulas are complex when their treatment has increased risk for incontinence (eg, crosses >30%-50% of the external anal sphincter, location of tract is anterior in a woman, has multiple tracts, is recurrent, there is preexisting incontinence, local irradiation, or Crohn's disease).

list.listitem: Fistulas are difficult to estimate as anal discomfort is most often self-attributed to hemorrhoids. In a random telephone survey of over 100 adults between the ages of 21 and 65 years, 20% had anorectal symptoms, and most had not consulted a physician.
In the Helsinki study of 510,000 persons between 1969 and 1978, investigators found an annual incidence of 8.6 per 100,000 people, of which 12.3 were for men and 5.6 for women.
Nonspecific with no underlying pathology (90%).
Postoperative and traumatic, including obstetrical (3%).
Anal fissure (3%).
Inflammatory bowel disease (3%).
Tuberculosis (<1%). In an endemic area, TB was diagnosed in 7 of 96 patients (7.3%) with anal fistula.
Other: anorectal malignancy, diverticulitis, radiation therapy, steroid therapy, HIV infection, actinomycosis, lymphogranuloma venereum, and leukemia.
Disease typically begins as an infection arising from the anal crypts; up to 50% of perianal abscesses result in fistulae.
After surgical or spontaneous drainage to the skin, an epithelialized (or granulation tissue-lined) tract develops, causing recurrent symptoms.

Common presenting symptoms include rectal pain, swelling, and persistent or intermittent discharge; less common presentations are bleeding, diarrhea, and fever. History of perianal abscess is common. C
A history of inflammatory bowel disease, immune suppression, or trauma should raise suspicion of complex fistula. C
The external opening may be evident or discovered when there is purulent discharge on exam; the internal opening may be noted on DRE or anoscopy and may require examination under anesthesia. C

On physical examination, anterior location or external openings more than 3 cm from the anal verge are more likely to be complex fistulae and warrant additional imaging ( eg, endoscopic ultrasound, MRI, CT, and fistulography). C
Fistulography is not sufficiently accurate and should be reserved for suspected fistulae to adjacent organs (eg, bladder). C

Differential.Differential_Features: Associated folliculitis, apocrine glands; does not communicate with the anal canal
Preceded by slow growing, nontender nodule when located in the genital region; internally does not communicate with the anal canal
Sacrococcygeal location; does not communicate with the anal canal
Labial location; does not communicate with the anal canal

list.listitem: History should include symptoms and past medical history to guide physical examination.
Common symptoms include rectal discharge (63%), rectal pain (34%-93%), and rectal swelling (24%-50%). Less commonly patients report rectal bleeding (10%-16%), diarrhea (5%), and fever (<5%).

On physical examination, patients may have chronic drainage (spontaneous or on DRE), pustule-like lesions, an open sinus, elevation of granulation tissue, and/or a fibrous tract or cord on DRE. Anoscopy can reveal an internal opening.

Examination may have to be under anesthesia if extremely painful. Examination under anesthesia includes visual inspection, palpation, and probing fistula tracks. Anal sphincter tone should be determined prior to examination under anaesthesia, and followed up with manometry, if abnormal, prior to surgery.

Physical techniques to identify the internal opening and the course of the fistula include injection of hydrogen peroxide, milk, or dilute methylene blue, watching for exit at the dentate line; traction on the external opening causing dimpling at the internal opening; and blunt probe of the external opening to help determine the direction of the tract (taking care not to create a false passage).

Goodsall's rule: Fistulae with an external opening anterior to a plane passing transversely through the center of the anus will follow a straight radial course to the dentate line. Fistulae with openings posterior to this line will follow a curved course to the posterior midline. Predictive accuracy is 49% for anterior tracts and 90% for posterior openings.
No laboratory tests are routinely indicated. Consider WBC if febrile.
Radiologic studies are not indicated for routine fistula evaluation; MRI provided additional information in only 8% of patients with primary fistulae.
Fistulography: Accuracy is 16% to 48%; this is generally reserved for patients in whom there is concern for fistula between the rectum and an adjacent organ (eg, bladder).
MRI: Concordance with surgical findings is 42% to 85% with 14-month follow-up as the gold standard. MRI is 89% sensitive, 69% specific, with LR+ 2.9, LR- 0.16.

Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS): Studies show mixed results when compared to MRI, depending on equipment used. EUS may be more sensitive than MRI for evaluating patients with Crohn's disease (concordance 82% with ultrasound vs. 50% with MRI). Use of MRI in complex tracts has been shown to decrease incidence of recurrence. B
CT scan: While valuable for identifying abscesses, CT scan is less accurate than endoanal ultrasound (24% vs. 82% ). Poor resolution makes classification of lesion unreliable.

Examination under anesthesia (EUA): When combined with endoanal ultrasound or MRI, the EUA is useful for classifying fistula in ano and Crohn's fistula. Accuracy of EUA combined with either ultrasound or MRI was 100% accurate in 1 study. Pelvic MRI or EUS combined with EUA changed surgical management in 10% to 15% of patients with Crohn's disease and 22% of patients without Crohn's disease.

Suspect anorectal fistula in patients with rectal pain, discharge, or bleeding. Physical examination is the mainstay of diagnosis with visual inspection and digital rectal examination (especially under anesthesia).
Risks for complex fistula include inflammatory bowel disease, anterior location, history of trauma (including obstetric), diabetes, and location >3 cm from the anal verge.
If high risk, consider endoanal ultrasound if available as first choice for imaging, followed by MRI (higher cost) or fistulography.
Add flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy if there is a history of inflammatory bowel disease, change in bowel habits, or rectal bleeding.
Initial management is symptomatic: sitz baths, analgesics, hygiene, and antidiarrheal agents. C
There are no controlled trials using antibiotics for simple fistulae. Antibiotics with or without immunomodulators are of moderate short-term benefit in patients with Crohn's disease. B

The approach to surgical management depends on the location of the fistula and symptoms. Options range from fistulotomy and curettage to seton, endoanal flap and fibrin glue or plug, diverting colostomy, and proctectomy. B
Based on limited evidence, no specific surgical technique appears more favorable than others for outcomes of postoperative pain, healing time, length of hospital stay, and quality of life. B

Initial management is symptomatic and includes analgesics (eg, acetaminophen, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) and antidiarrheal agents, if indicated. Options for the latter include bismuth subsalicylate (Kaopectate), 2 caplets or 30 mL every 8 hours as needed, and diphenoxylate/atropine sulphate (Lomotil), 2 tabs or 10 mL four times daily as needed, taking care to avoid constipation.
Topical analgesics (eg, lidocaine) provide temporary relief but may be sensitizing and cause further irritation and inflammation.
Antibiotics (eg, metronidazole, ciprofloxacin) and/or immunomodulators ( eg, infliximab, 6 mercaptopurine, azathioprine, cyclosporine, tacrolimus) have been used in refractory Crohn's disease.,

Other indications for antibiotics include valvular heart disease, extensive soft tissue involvement, necrotizing infection, cellulitis, sepsis, and immunocompromise, including diabetes, malnutrition, cancer (especially leukemia or lymphoma), and AIDS.
No therapy is initially necessary for asymptomatic fistula such as those found on routine rectal examination; up to 38% resolve spontaneously.
Goal of surgical treatment is to remove the fistula while preserving function. Approach depends on type and location of fistula.
Intersphincteric: Primary fistulotomy, curette of the base, is left open to heal by secondary intention.

Transsphincteric: If low, primary fistulotomy may be indicated. If high, cutting seton (suture) allows for division of the sphincter with simultaneous closure behind by scarring: partial fistulectomy (removal of tract only from external opening to the sphincteric muscles) combined with seton and/or with endoanal flap and fibrin glue.

Suprasphincteric, extrasphincteric, and complex: Use non-cutting seton with plug or glue combined with immunomodulator (if associated with inflammatory bowel disease), staged procedures with cutting setons, and endoanal flaps.

In a Cochrane review of 10 studies of surgery for anorectal fistula, there were no major difference between the various techniques used as far as recurrence rates with the exception of a higher recurrence rate in the glue plus flap group vs. flap only technique. The Fibrin glue and advancement flap procedure studies, however, report low incontinence rates.

In the presence of perianal abscess with fistula, fistula repair with abscess drainage significantly reduced recurrence, persistent abscess/fistula, and repeat surgery compared with abscess drainage alone.
Consider diverting ileostomy for severe active Crohn's disease.
Proctectomy is the treatment of last resort.
Radiofrequency fistulotomy has a recurrence/failure rate as low as 1.5%.

Collagen plug placement and autologous transplant with adipose-derived stem cells are experimental treatments. In 1 Chinese RCT (N = 90) comparing acellular dermal matrix (ADM) with endorectal advancement flap in complex anorectal fistula, healing rates (82% vs. 64% ), fistula recurrence (2 vs. 13 patients), and postoperative pain time were significantly better with ADM. ADM dislodgement occurred in 5 patients and there were no differences in incontinence or anal deformity.
Sitz baths, local hygiene (cleansing with warm soap and water), and high-fiber diet are all routinely recommended but their effectiveness is unproved.
A cohort study followed 300 Polish patients for a mean of 4.2 years; investigators found a recurrence of fistulae in 14.3% and gas or stool incontinence in 10.7%. B
Recurrence rate was 5.4% in patients with primary fistula, 51.7% in patients with a recurrent fistula, 12% with single-tract fistula, and 32.4% with multi-tract fistula. B
In 136 patients, fistulotomy in patients with classic Crohn's disease resulted in 89% healing with preservation of continence; in patients with active colitis, this occurred in only 26.6%. B
Malignant transformation (most commonly adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma) may occur in rare cases of chronic perineal fistulas in patients with Crohn's disease. B

In a case series of 112 children with perianal abscess and fistula-in-ano, most (86.6%) were cured with conservative treatment (local care, sitz baths, incision and drainage (67%), antibiotics if systemic illness) in 5.2 + 3.9 months from illness onset.
